idiom_name: data class PersonRow + PersonRow.update(conn) over JDBC PreparedStatement
implementation_notes: A data class mirrors the row and small extension functions or a gateway object perform the JDBC work: a companion find(conn, id) using PreparedStatement and a row-filling factory, plus update/insert functions that bind the properties. Kotlin's use { } extension replaces try-with-resources and named/default arguments keep the constructor readable; nothing in the standard library replaces the gateway, so the classic structure is written out - which is what you want when the SQL must stay explicit and the row must stay a plain value.
pitfalls: A data class is a value: copy() produces a new instance, so 'mutate then save' must operate on the same reference the caller updates or the change is lost.
JDBC Connection/PreparedStatement are not thread-safe; sharing one across coroutines requires an explicit dispatcher and connection confinement.

variants.name: JetBrains Exposed DAO Entity with insert/flush/delete
variants.implementation_notes: Exposed's DAO layer provides one Entity object per row: an EntityClass companion acts as the finder (PersonEntity[id], PersonEntity.all()), property delegates map columns, and the entity persists itself through insert(), flush() (dirty-field update) and delete() inside a transaction. It is the library-provided version of this pattern on the JVM/Kotlin side; note that Exposed also keeps an identity map per transaction, so entities are cached and shared, which is more than the classic gateway promises.
pitfalls: An Exposed entity is bound to the transaction that created it; keeping a reference beyond transaction { } leads to a stale or leaking object.
EntityClass caches entities per transaction, so two lookups return the same instance - code that relied on the gateway's fresh-object semantics must be adjusted.
